summary: The United States Department of the Interior submitted a formal comment letter on the Bad Creek Draft Environmental Impact Statement, raising concerns across multiple areas including fish and wildlife resources, minerals and groundwater hydrology, outdoor recreation, and cultural resources. The Department conditionally withheld endorsement of the project, insisting that adverse impacts on the Lake Jocassee two-story fishery and Howard Creek trout fishery must be mitigated before full support could be given. The letter also called for corrections to trail nomenclature, improved discussion of mineral resources and groundwater, better recreation alternatives analysis, and compliance with cultural resource preservation procedures.
complaint_summary: The Department of the Interior raised multiple concerns about the draft EIS, including incomplete data on project impacts to the Lake Jocassee two-story fishery and Howard Creek trout fishery, inadequate discussion of mineral resources and groundwater, misleading trail nomenclature and recreation alternatives ranking, and insufficient cultural resource survey compliance, and withheld full endorsement of the project pending assurance that adverse impacts would be mitigated.

statement.text:
Dear Mr. Plumb:
The Department of the Interior has received and reviewed the draft environmental statement for the Bad Creek Project (FPC No. 2740) as transmitted by your September 30, 1975, letter. We have the following comments arranged by areas of Departmental jurisdiction and expertise.
Fish and Wildlife Resources
In general the draft statement adequately addresses projectimpacts on fish and wildlife resources. However, there two major areas for which data are incomplete and which the statement fails to describe and evaluate. These are:
1. Project impact on the development of a two-story fishery in Lake Jocassee, and
2. Project impact on Howard Creek's trout fishery due to flow reductions in Bad Creek.
On October 8, 1974, this Department commented on the license application. We recommended that studies of these two potential adverse impacts be completed and mitigation plans be prepared to compensate for the anticipated losses. We further recommended that this work be completed within one year after license issuance.
Unfortunately the draft statement does not bring the reader up to date on these studies and does not give any indication of whether or not the recommended timeframe for completion will be met. Pages 3-19 through 3-20 attempt to list and analyze project impacts on the Lake Jocassee fishery. Three of the eight items are not impacts but merely statements of fact concerning the project. This would be a good place to insert a status report on the two-story fishery impact study.
See revised Sections 2.2.2.2, 3.2.2.3, and 4 and 9.
No comment required.

On page 3-23 we are again only partially informed as to progress on the Howard Creek flow augmentation study. The paragraph also minimizes the potential adverse impact to the Howard Creek fishery if flow augmentation is not provided. The final statement should correct this.
Pages 4-2 and 4-3 are also inadequate in their discussion of these studies and should be revised in the final statement to acknowledge if the studies will be completed within one year of the license issuance. Page 4-3 also states: "The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service plans to study the impact of pumping operations on the fishery resources of Lake Jocassee." The FWS has ongoing studies in the area, but they do not replace either of the applicant's studies as discussed above. Since there is a potential for misunderstanding, we recommend that the sentence be altered or deleted in the final statement.
The Department cannot fully endorse this project until it has some assurance that these adverse impacts will be mitigated. It appears from the draft statement that our October 8, 1974, recommendations are not yet an integral part of the licensing process so we reemphasize them here for adequate disposition in the final statement and license document.
Minerals and Groundwater Hydrology
In recent years, mineral production from Oconee County has been limited to small quantities of crushed stone. The project site lies within the Chattooga zone of the crystalline region, a narrow belt of granitic rocks containing deposits of gold, lead, soapstone, graphite, mica, feldspar, and corundum. Although no mines are currently in operation, gold, lead, mica, and corundum have been produced in the past.
The statement contains a brief description of the geology of the area but no mention of mineral resources or the impact of this project on such resources. We believe the statement must put on record what potential mineral resources might be involved in the project. The statement should also indicate whether or not a mineral resource survey has been made.
We find that although drinking water for domestic and recreational facilities is to be obtained largely from wells and springs (page 1-8), no description of the occurrence of groundwater in the area is given nor are impacts addressed. Outdoor Recreation
On page 1-14 of the subject document, reference is made to the Appalachian Foothills Trail. The trail described in the statement and pertinent to applicant's proposed trail is referred to as the Cherokee Foothills Trail, the Carolina Foothills Trail, or the Foothills Trail. To our knowledge, it has never been called the Appalachian Foothills Trail except in the draft impact statement. To the extent that the nomenclature is not widely used, it may be misleading to readers not familiar with the route description.
Section 1.4.1 has been revised to reflect the prevalent nomenclature.
In comparing recreation potential at the alternative pumped storage sites, the references to a numerical order of recreation potential is misleading and uninformative unless the basis of the ranking system is also discussed. If the ordering is used to describe recreation aspects of the alternative sites, it should be accompanied with discussion of the system and specific references to recreation related data and social data for the sites. If the system is not used, the Recreation sections can be improved with greater reference to specific recreation related data for the sites.
Sections 8.3.1.5, 8.3.2.5, and 8.3.3.5 have been revised.
Cultural Resources
The comments of the State Historic Preservation Officer should appear in the final statement.
See letters, Lee to Plumb 8/19/74 and 3/24/75.
4.2.3. History and Archeology
This section is not supported by data included in the statement. On page 2-71 (2.5.2) it is noted that the route of the proposed transmission line was not surveyed for cultural resources. The section should be rewritten to conform to actual knowledge based on field surveys.
This section has been revised. Applicant has proposed archeological surveys for the transmission line corridor.
9.5 Archeology
The purpose of field surveys during the early stages in project planning is to locate resources and to allow for time to take

steps to comply with cultural resource preservation procedures including the consideration of modifying construction locations. Waiting to make required surveys until just prior to construction is not in compliance with the intent of cultural resource preservation procedures. If historical and archeological resources are significant as implied by this section, then the final statement should summarize the survey findings and describe the procedures that will be undertaken to comply with 36 CFR 800.
See Staff recommendation in Section 9.
We hope these comments will be of assistance in preparing the final environmental statement.
Sincerely yours,
Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Interior
Honorable Kenneth F. Plumb Secretary Federal Power Commission Washington, D. C. 20426
